In January 2025, Liberux, a startup based in Madrid, Spain, announced its upcoming NEXX Linux phone based on the RK3588S with specs to make nerds salivate: 4×2.4GHz Cortex-A76, 4x Cortex-A55, Mali-G610 MP4 GPU, 32GB LPDDR4X RAM, 256GB eMMC, 5G modem and 3 hardware kill switches. In June 2025, Liberux started the crowdfunding for the phone, and a couple days later announced a modular and open architecture that would allow the RAM board with an FPC connector to be upgraded up to 32GB, the eMMC board with a standard socket to be upgraded up to 512GB, and the cellular modem with a custom adapter board to be replaced/upgraded. The price varied between €790 and €1310, depending on the selected configuration. In addition, the NEXX would have two USB-C 3.1 ports to facilitate the phone being used a convergent desktop PC and an AW8737SCSR amplifier and a 3.5mm audio jack for better analog audio.

The NEXX was a revolutionary design, promising to be the first phone in history with two USB ports and the first one with the RAM and eMMC on separate boards, so it could be upgraded and connected like a normal PC. Liberux was attempting to offer the first truly convergent smartphone that had the right software and hardware to replace a desktop PC, yet it hardly generated any headlines in the tech press. It only got 120 pre-orders in a month, which generated a tenth of the $1.7 million in crowdfunding that it needed. When its crowdfunding campaign failed, Liberux reported that it was negotiating with investors for raise the funds to build a prototype. However, its last post on the company’s Mastadon account was in November 2025 about “moving forward with new self-funding.” After 11 months of silence, it is looking increasingly doubtful that the NEXX will ever come to market.

There is more hope for the Dawndrums Divine D. phone, which is being produced by a startup in Tunisia. The startup has continued to make slow progress according to its Mastodon posts. They are now on the second revision of their main board and have produced a breakout board for debugging it. They are developing their own distro known as DawnOS, which is based on Mobian and planning to support both the Phosh and Plasma Mobile interfaces. They are asking for donations, but appear to be largely self funded at this point. Like the NEXX, the Divine D. also promises to be an outstanding convergent phone, supporting up to 32GB RAM and offering a separate HDMI port for video out. It also offers a LoRa (long-range radio) chip, and a pogo pin interface to add accessories to the phone.
Jolla shows that there is still demand for Linux phones

While the failed crowdfunding of the Liberux NEXX and the limited sales of the Furi Labs FLX1 would suggest that there isn’t much hope for Linux phones, it is important to keep in mind that these phones were poorly advertised and produced by unknown startups that had no prior track record, so people were reluctant to order them. Bitter experience with the Librem 5 refunds, the failures of the PinePhone Pro, and all the cancelled Linux mobile devices over the years, such as the Ubuntu Edge in 2013, the Firefox OS phones in 2015, the Jolla Tablet in 2015 and the Necunos NC_1 in 2019, has taught Linux enthusiasts to be cautious about crowdfunding mobile devices.

However, there are reasons to believe that there is quite a bit of pent-up demand for mobile Linux, and it only requires the right kind of promotion and a company with a credible track record to unlock it. Ironically, the company demonstrating that people still want to use Linux phones is tiny Jolla, which has somehow managed to survive over the years.

The Finnish engineers who used to work on Nokia’s MeeGo founded their own company named Jolla Oy in 2011 to keep developing that code as Sailfish OS. They took the FOSS parts of MeeGo and added their proprietary Silica interface based on Qt QML, which imitates the Swipe UI that Nokia had developed for Meego on the N900/N9. They also developed their own proprietary AlienDalvik to run Android apps inside Linux. Jolla deserves credit for developing libhybris and helping to maintain much of the code developed by Nokia, including the oFono telephony library and the Maliit virtual keyboard. Remarkably, the small Finnish company managed to survive nearly going bankrupt in late 2015, when it cancelled its crowdfunded Jolla Tablet, which caused many of its customers who preordered to lose their money. It split off its hardware operations into a separate company named Jolla-Devices, which sells now Sony smartphones with Sailfish OS preinstalled to the European market, plus Volla Phones with Ubuntu Touch and Pixels with GrapheneOS.

After killing off the original company in 2024, because it was majority owned by Russian investors, who were politically toxic due to the war in Ukraine, Jolla reemerged under a new company named JollaBoys that bought the old company’s assets from Jolla Oy. The new Jolla company has returned to the business of selling hardware. Jolla announced its Jolla C2 Community Phone in May 2024, and started delivering them two months later, which helped reestablish the credibility of the company. When Jolla started taking preorders for its new Jolla Phone on December 5, 2025, it sold out its crowdfunding goal of 2000 phones within the first 48 hours and 5000 phones within the first week. People were pre-ordering the Jolla Phone without having seen any reviews of the phone and not even knowing what processor it would contain. The phone, which initially cost $499 and now costs was €679, was marketed as containing 12GB RAM, 256GB storage, a user-replaceable battery and a physical privacy switch. Jolla’s advertising for the phone clearly struck a chord with European consumers, which proclaimed it to be a “Do It Together (DIT) Linux phone, shaped by the people who use it.” The Finnish company emphasized the independence of the phone from the rest of the mobile phone industry, stating on the order page: “The Jolla Phone is not based on Big Tech technology. It is governed by European privacy thinking and a community-led model.”

Jolla has sold 15,000 units of its phone as of August 2026 just by taking pre-orders for production batches from its web site, and it probably could have sold far more units if it had paid for advertising, expanded beyond the European market, and kept the phone in stock, so customers didn’t have to wait months for the next production batch. Clearly, there is an untapped market of people who are dissatisfied with the reigning Android/iOS duopoly.
The mobile industry is shutting down the AOSP alternative

Today the use of Linux is growing on the desktop. Many people are installing Linux on their PCs, because they have become disgusted by how Microsoft has turned Windows into an advertising platform for surveillance capitalism and a vehicle for AI slop. Rather than buying new PCs, a growing number of people have decided to install Linux, because support for Windows 10 has ended and they can’t upgrade their old PCs to Windows 11 due to Microsoft’s arbitrary TPM restrictions.

Likewise, many people are equally disenchanted with Android and iOS on their phones. More people have grown distrustful of the surveillance capitalism which undergirds the Android market and the restrictions and rising prices of Apple’s “walled garden” on the iPhone, yet the options to escape the smartphone duopoly keep shrinking. In the past, people who wanted to gain some control over their digital lives could unlock the bootloader on their phone and install an AOSP derivative such as LineageOS, /e/OS, CalyxOS or GrapheneOS, however the mobile phone industry is increasingly shutting off this escape valve.

Every year there are fewer Android phone models on the market which allow the bootloader to be unlocked. The rise of Chinese brands, which now control roughly 60% of the global smartphone market, has driven many of the traditional phones brands out of the market which did allow their bootloaders to be unlocked. Many of the phone brands that were mod-friendly, such as LG, BQ, LeEco, WileyFox, Essential and Razer, are now gone from the market, and other mod-friendly brands like Sony and HTC now have so few sales that they are no longer relevant in the global smartphone market. Huawei stopped allowing its bootloaders to be unlocked in 2018. In the last couple years, Samsung, ASUS and Realme all followed Huawei’s bad example and no longer allow their bootloaders to be unlocked. Xiaomi, which rose to fame as a mod-friendly brand, has recently implemented so many restrictions to obtain its unlock codes, that it is unlikely that modders will bother porting custom ROMs to future Xiaomi models.

As noted in my article on LineageOS statistics, the brands which have good policies for bootloader unlocking has shrunk from 42.5% to about 7% of the global smartphone market over the last couple years. The brands which allow their bootloaders to be unlocked (without major restrictions like Xiaomi) only sold about 87 million phones in 2025, including Lenovo/Motorola (60M), Google (12M), OnePlus (11.6M), Nothing (2M), GigaSet (>1M), Sony (400k), Fairphone (145k), SHIFT (10k), Teracube, Volla and Brax. Together those brands only represent 7% of the 1245.5 million total smartphones sold in 2025.

However, that is an overestimate, since most phone models never get good custom ROMs made for them. A good portion of Motorola and Google phones are sold through carriers, and many carriers like Verizon don’t allow their phones to ever be unlocked, even if they are no longer under contract. MediaTek Dimensity and UNISOC Tiger processors have gained market share in recent years, and those chipmakers don’t publish the source code for their kernels like Qualcomm does for its Snapdragon processors. A few brands that use MediaTek SoC’s, such as Motorola, Xiaomi, Volla, Gigaset, TeraCube and Brax, do publish their kernel code, but that code for many other MediaTek phones will never get published, nor will custom ROMs be made for them. UNISOC processors are basically black boxes for the modding community. The bootloaders of all phones with Apple A-series, Huawei Kirin and recent Samsung Exynos processors are locked, so the modding community is restricted to just Qualcomm Snapdragon, Google Tensor and some MediaTek Dimensity processors. Motorola and Xiaomi have switched most of their budget model lines from Snapdragon to MediaTek Dimensity processors, so they are harder to mod.

Aside from the Motorola Moto G05, which was released in Jan 2025 and replaced 8 months later by the G06, there has not been a single budget phone released by a major phone maker in 2025 or 2026 that has gained official support by LineageOS. Gaining official LineageOS support is important, because many of the other custom ROMs are based on LineageOS and only port to its officially supported models. Just looking at phone models with official LineageOS support which allow their bootloaders to be unlocked, only about 20 million or 2% of smarphones sold each year are good for installing custom ROMs.

The situation is about to get much worse. Sadly, Oppo just announced that it will pull its OnePlus brand from the North American and European markets. OnePlus phones will still be sold in India and China (where the bootloader can be unlocked if the user presents an official Chinese ID card), but OnePlus is essentially gone for the modding community. Nothing, which was a rising star in the modding world, has been losing sales. The London-based company denies rumors that it will pull out of a third of the countries where it currently sells phones, but confirms that it plans to cut 100 jobs, which comprise 12% of its workforce. At any rate, none of the phones which Nothing has released in the last two years have gained official LineageOS support.
Samsung has been making it more and more difficult to mod its phones over the last decade, so the Korean company’s decision to lock the bootloader for all its phones getting its ONE UI 8 interface wasn’t a surprise, but Xiaomi’s decision to start restricting its bootloader unlock codes was a major blow for the modding community. The only major global brand left for modding is Motorola, but there are only unofficial ports available for recent Motorola models, meaning that some things don’t work correctly or security patches aren’t being provided. Motorola promises to launch phones with GrapheneOS in 2027, but they will be flagship models which probably cost over $1000 and be limited to a few select countries.

Aside from the Motorola Moto G15 (released in December 2024), people are unlikely to find a new phone where they can install an official LineageOS port for sale in Africa, most of Latin America (except Mexico) and most of Asia (except India, Japan, Taiwan, Singapore and Malaysia). The only option to run a custom ROM in most of the world is to buy a used Motorola or Xiaomi phone from a couple years ago, such as the Moto G (2024), Moto G32, Moto G34, Moto G84, POCO F5, POCO F5 Pro, POCO F6 Pro or Redmi Note 13 Pro. There are more recent phones like the Moto Edge 70, which have unofficial LineageOS ports, but it is a gamble if they will ever be officially supported by LineageOS.

As Google has pushed phone makers to support their phones for longer, many companies have decided to collect more personal data from their users for better targeted advertising and for training artificial intelligences. The smartphone industry is moving away from a business model based on planned obsolescence toward one based on surveillance capitalism, and the phone makers don’t want their users to opt out of the system, so they have removed the option to unlock the bootloader and made it harder to gain root access. That way they can recoup the cost of providing more years of support for their phones by monetizing their users’ data.

In addition, Google has made it harder to maintain custom ROMs, because it has moved more and more functionality from AOSP into its proprietary libraries and services (starting with Android 4.1 in 2012), and largely abandoned the development of many of the free/open source apps in AOSP in favor of its proprietary apps. Starting with AOSP 16 in 2025, Google stopped including the device trees and driver binaries for Pixel devices in AOSP, so ROM developers no longer had target devices, where they could easily test out and adapt the latest versions of AOSP on running hardware. Now custom ROM developers have to do painful trial and error to make the device trees for Pixel phones just like all the other phone brands. Google also squashed the kernel’s commit history, which makes it very difficult for ROMs like GrapheneOS to create their own custom kernels, because they can’t easily take new features, bug fixes and security patches from Google’s kernels.

Given how the smartphone industry is locking down their hardware and pushing business models that are inimical to users’ privacy, there is increased opportunity for Linux phones to be marketed to people who want to escape the Android/iOS duopoly and surveillance capitalism.
Three types of Linux phones are now possible

In the past, it was much harder to bring a Linux phone to market, but now there are three viable types of Linux phones that can be brought to market, and all of them have better prospects than in the past. The first type is the pure Linux phone which runs a Linux kernel, like the Librem 5, Liberty, PinePhone and PinePhone Pro. These phones previously didn’t have the processing power to offer the functionality that people expect in a smartphone. They often lacked components such image signal processors, audio digital signal processors, hardware video encoders, Vulkan graphics, neural processors and encryption engines, or they lacked the FOSS drivers to support those components. The RK3588S and the upcoming RK3668, however, will give pure Linux phones the processing power to be viable alternatives to Android and iOS phones for the first time.

The pure Linux phone is the riskiest type because it requires the most investment in engineering the hardware. Companies can’t just modify a reference phone design from Qualcomm or MediaTek or call up a phone ODM and ask them to modify one of their existing designs. They have to work with a design house or ODM that has some experience with radio frequencies to custom design a phone with 2 to 3 times more components than a standard smartphone. This means many iterations of the circuit board to get it right, and some kernel work to use all those different chips. It will take a long time to get to market, which can lead to customer complaints and reputational loss if using crowdfunding to finance the dev work.

The benefit of the pure Linux approach is that it allows for true hardware kill switches that cut the current to separate components, rather than the use of pins on an integrated mobile SoC or software to turn off the WiFi/Bluetooth, cellular modem and GPS/GNSS. The second benefit is the ability to select components that have free/open source drivers, which allows for greater software freedom and more transparency to address security and privacy concerns. The use of proprietary blobs in the drivers often prevents the kernel from being upgraded because the blobs are often only compatible with a specific kernel version number, which allows the chipmakers to dictate the lifespan of devices. Another benefit of not using a reference design from an SoC maker or an ODM is the phone maker has full control over the design and can publish the schematics and board views for the circuit boards, so the hardware is as free as the software.

In the past, Qualcomm didn’t produce powerful Internet of Things processors with Linux support, but now it is possible to build a good Linux phone based on an Internet of Things processor, like the QCM6490 or QCM8850 with an integrated cellular modem. These Dragonwing processors are not as up-to-date as the latest Snapdragon processors, but most of them receive 10 years or 15 years of software support, and many of them will eventually get partial support in mainline Linux, so they can live on with community support after they are no longer supported by Qualcomm.

The third kind of Linux phone is built on an integrated mobile SoC, which runs a standard Linux stack on top of an Android kernel using libhybris to translate glib calls to Android’s Bionic. This used to not be a good option because Android SoC’s were not supported long enough for the long development cycles and lower annual sales of Linux phones, but now it is possible for the high-end processors that are getting 8 years of software support from Qualcomm and MediaTek.

This approach is the most economical way to bring a Linux phone to market, since many phone ODMs already have reference models available and are willing to work with phone sellers to tweak those models to their specifications. It is not impossible to work with an ODM to add privacy switches to a design, as Furi Labs demonstrated with its FLX1, but it takes longer to get a custom design to market, so it is important to select an SoC that gets 7 or 8 years of software support, so the phone will enjoy a reasonable lifespan.

It is no longer necessary for Linux phone companies to expend huge amounts of capital in developing mobile Linux, because there are now three good mobile interfaces—Phosh, Plasma Mobile and Lomiri—which offer a reasonably complete complement of applications, so hardware companies don’t need to risk bankruptcy developing the software like before. Because Phosh and now Plasma Mobile are based on a well-supported desktop stack and convergent applications, they will require much less work to maintain and it is easier and less costly to keep providing software updates for the phone. Companies offering Linux phones will still need to hire developers to work on things like power management and camera support, but they don’t have to bet the farm like Purism did with the Librem 5 or provide no software support as PINE64 did with the PinePhone and PinePhone Pro.

This reduction in software development costs, however, probably won’t result in more economical Linux phones. The shorter software support for the QMC4490 and the mid-range and low range Snapdragon and Dimensity processors rules out the making of an economical Linux phone. It is possible to make an upper mid-range Linux phone based on a Snapdragon 7 or Dimensity 8000 series processor, but it won’t support video out via DisplayPort Alt Mode over USB-C, so it can’t be used as a convergent PC, which is a major selling point for Linux phones. Given that the QMC6490 does support DisplayPort Alt Mode, it is probably the best option for making an upper mid-range phone.

Companies like Jolla, Furi Labs, Volla and Brax may choose to continue making mid-range Linux phones, but they will likely suffer from the same problem as the FLX1 and C2, where the Android kernel is unsupported and no longer getting security updates, so it is better to move up to a more expensive SoC that gets 8 years of support. Ideally, these companies will stop using MediaTek processors, and select Snapdragon processors that get partially supported in mainline Linux, so people can run a distro like Nura on them after they are no longer supported.
The real barrier holding back Linux phones is the companies

Now that the available SoC’s and software are no longer holding back the making of compelling Linux phones, the real barrier to creating a viable Linux phone market are the companies to make and sell those phones. There aren’t many companies with the experience and passion to make Linux phones, which historically have lost money.

PINE64 recently announced that it is pausing production of most of its devices due to the high prices of RAM and eMMC. Essentially PINE64 is admitting that it can’t raise the price of many of its products, because they don’t have the needed software support, so many people won’t pay elevated prices for them. It appears unlikely at this point that PINE64 will change its business model to pay for software developers to work on the kernels for its hardware, nor is it repairing its relationship with the distributions and volunteer developers who have abandoned the company, so it is unlikely to ever produce the rumored PinePhone 2 using the RK3566. In theory another community-based Linux hardware company could arise, that charges a bit more so it has the necessary funds to pay developers to work on the kernel support for the hardware, but it appears highly unlikely that another community-based hardware company like PINE64 will appear.

In contrast, Purism is clearly planning to produce a second version of its phone. In its July 2026 newsletter, Purism stated that it “is in the early stages of planning the Librem 5 v2 and Liberty 5 v2.” It is preparing a “crowdfunding campaign in the coming months” to “gauge customer interest and traction, which will help fund the production of our second version.” The problem is that Purism’s public reputation has been stained by its refusal to refund the Librem 5 backers who cancelled their orders. Refunding the 600 customers who are still waiting for their Librem 5 refunds would do a lot to restore the company’s public reputation, and it would cost the company less than $400k. Without taking that step, it seems unlikely that Purism will be able to crowdfund the “over $2 million” that it projects will be needed to produce its next Linux phone. Maybe Purism can charge a lesser amount (such as $99) to pre-order the phone, and then use those numbers to raise capital privately to develop the phone.

At any rate, the time and cost of producing the Librem 5 v2 will be much less than the first version of the phone, because Phosh and its applications have already been developed and the mainline Linux driver support for the RK3588S is already in a good state due to the last four years of work by Collabora. Hopefully, Purism will either provide funding or developers to help Collabora get the ISP and hardware video encoding working.

The challenge for Purism is that it also needs to finance the development of its next generation of Librem 14 notebook, Librem 11 tablet and Librem Mini. The Librem 11 and Mini are rebadged ODM designs, so they don’t require as much work, but the Librem 14 is a custom design, which requires quite a bit more work and financing to create. In addition, Purism reported in its July newsletter that it has been pre-approved to get over $50 million in funding from the CHIPS Act to develop a Librem Core-V processor based on the RISC-V architecture, which will be a huge undertaking for the tiny company which doesn’t have any prior experience in chip design. Presumably, Purism will have to raise some matching funds to get the government funding for its chip project. In other words, many projects will be competing for Purism’s attention in the future, and the Librem 5 v2 could be neglected and postponed in favor of other products.

Presumably Dawndrums will launch a crowdfunding campaign once it has a working prototype of its RK3588S-based phone to show to the public, but the company based in Tunis has been very tight lipped about its future plans to bring the phone to market. There has been no news from Furi Labs about a new phone model to follow the FLX1s+. The implementation of Ubuntu Touch on the BraX3 phone has been stalled for months, and it appears that Brax Technologies is depending on the UBports community to finish the porting work. Volla Phone continues to offer Ubuntu Touch as an alternative operating system on its phones, but the German company’s primary focus is on developing its own Volla OS, which is an AOSP derivative oriented toward privacy.

Jolla is making the right moves to create a viable Linux phone market. The Finnish company says that it plans to move to mass production of its Jolla Phone, so the phone will be in stock, and to offer the phone to the North American market. However, many in the Linux community will be reluctant to embrace Jolla’s phones, because of the proprietary software in its Silica interface and its AppSupport (aka AlienDalvik) to run Android apps. People who believe in free and open source software won’t want to buy a phone from a company that has been violating the GPL 2.0 license by not published the kernel code for its Jolla C2 and Jolla Phone. In addition, these phones use UNISOC and MediaTek processors that don’t have any mainline Linux support, and they will probably have short lifespans, since their kernel are unlikely to ever be upgraded.

A critical factor in the success of Linux phones is publicizing the phones to attract the niche customers who care about Linux, software freedom, privacy or security. Liberux appears to have failed because it did such a poor job of publicizing its future NEXX phone and didn’t attract enough crowdfunding. Furi Labs similarly has done a very poor job of publicizing its phone, so that most Linux enthusiasts have never heard of the phone. Likewise, Dawndrums has done a very poor job of publicizing it development work on a future RK3588S phone. In contrast, Jolla has very effectively used social media to market its Jolla Phone to European customers.

There are several dozen companies that sell Linux PCs, which could potentially expand into the Linux phone market. Most of those companies, however, don’t have experience in the design of custom hardware. Most of them use standard notebook designs from one of the ODM’s that make specialty notebooks such as Clevo or Tongfang. Most of these companies also don’t have much experience doing kernel work, so they are probably better off just using a standard Android design provided by a phone ODM and installing Linux on top of Halium, so they can use a well-tested Android kernel and drivers.

There are also a number of companies that make Linux single board computers (SBC’s), who could potentially jump into the Linux phone market. They have more experience in working with Chinese and Taiwanese companies to design and produce custom hardware. They are better equipped to undertake the engineering challenges of entering the Linux phone market, but most of them do a poor job of engaging the community. Many companies which sell Linux SBC’s don’t have public forums for their customers and do a poor job of using social media and online advertising to promote their products.

Public opinion surveys show that people are increasingly aware that they are losing their privacy online. Ipsos polls found that 79% of global respondants and 84% of American respondants express worry about their online privacy. A Malwarebytes survey found that 89% of consumers are concerned regarding corporate and AI data misuse. 62% of Americans in a YouGov poll report worrying about how much personal data third parties have about them online. If Linux phones can be created that provide the same functionality and ease of use as Android or iOS phones, they could tap into that huge potential market of consumers who wish to preserve their privacy online. In order to appeal to mainstream users, Linux phones will need to support the usage of Android apps through Waydroid or a similar solution. In the same way that Murena and iodé sell AOSP phones which block third party trackers, Linux phones need to incorporate similar software.

The conditions may be ripe for Linux phones, but it is unclear whether the companies selling Linux phones will take advantage of those conditions to create a viable alternative to the current Android/iOS duopoly. For the sake of software freedom, online privacy and the greater longevity of mobile devices, a concerted push is needed to promote mobile Linux.

The SoC dilemma: weak but long lived vs powerful but short lived

The new option of Linux phones using a Qualcomm IoT SoC

The problem of using an Android kernel in a Linux phone

Why software was a major challenge for the Librem 5

The success of Phosh despite its limited funding

Adoption of mobile interfaces by Linux distros

PINE64's attempt to get around the cost of developing software

The waning enthusiasm for Linux phones

Jolla shows that there is still demand for Linux phones

The mobile industry is shutting down the AOSP alternative

Three types of Linux phones are now possible

The real barrier holding back Linux phones is the companies

Five years ago, Linux phones looked like they were poised to become a viable alternative to the Android/iOS duopoly that has an iron grip on the mobile phone industry. Sadly, after a brief flash of activity and community engagement with the release of the Purism Librem 5 and the PINE64 PinePhone in 2020, the Linux phone market has generally stagnated. This stagnation occurred partly because of the problems at Purism and PINE64, but also because the available Linux SoC’s weren’t up to the task of running a modern smartphone, and the hardware industry wasn’t providing any good alternatives with good free/open source drivers. In addition, Plasma Mobile and Phosh were still inchoate mobile interfaces at the time, and there wasn’t a good distro option to run these interfaces on Android kernels with a normal integrated mobile SoC. The poor performance of the PinePhone and Librem 5 and the problems with the PinePhone Pro and the Librem 5 refunds sapped people’s enthusiasm and willingness to take a chance on the next Linux phone.

Fortunately, all of these conditions are changing, and I believe that there is now the possibility that Linux could finally become a viable alternative to Google’s Android and Apple’s iOS in the mobile space, just like desktop Linux has become a viable alternative to Windows and Mac OSX on the PC over the last three decades. This isn’t to say that mobile Linux will fundamentally challenge the business of Google or Apple, but the conditions are ripe for a small market to arise for Linux phones, similar to the way that people can currently buy Linux PCs from a number of small companies, such as TUXEDO, System76, Purism, Slimbook, ThinkPenguin, Ubuntushop.biz, Entroware, Star Labs, Juno, Laptop with Linux, Linux Certified, ArkPC, etc.

It isn’t impossible that one of the big phone brands might sell a few models of phones with mobile Linux in the future, just like Lenovo and Dell currently sell a few PC models with Linux preinstalled in some limited markets. Motorola just announced that it will start selling some high-end phone models with GrapheneOS in 2027, which indicates that Google will allow the big phone makers to sell alternatives, probably because it fears anti-trust regulation. As the mobile industry increasingly shuts down the ability to unlock the bootloaders of Android phones, more people will be looking for an alternative to AOSP derivatives, and mobile Linux could provide that alternative.

Five years ago, it looked like mobile Linux had finally arrived. The Purism Librem 5 and PINE64 PinePhone had just been released, and even a big tech reviewer like Linus Tech Tips was trying them out. Mrwhosetheboss’s video, “Are Linux Smartphones about to KILL Android?,” where he held up the Librem 5, got 7.8 million views on YouTube. The Librem 5 had been ported to Mobian and postmarketOS, and the PinePhone had been ported to 20 different Linux distributions. There was a growing number of phone models that could run Jolla’s Sailfish OS and Ubuntu Touch on top of Android kernels, and many people were testing postmarketOS on their old phones. Plasma Mobile and Phosh were advancing fast as mobile interfaces. KDE had adopted Kirigami and GNOME was adopting Adwaita, so both KDE and GNOME apps could become adaptive between desktop and mobile interfaces. The Waydroid project was making it possible to run Android apps inside a Linux container. The future seemed bright for mobile Linux, but that future never seemed to arrive. It is worth examining what held back mobile Linux to understand how those conditions can be overcome in the future.

There has been great deal of experimentation with different mobile operating systems based on a Linux kernel over the last 25 years since the first mobile Linux devices were released—the Sharp Zaurus, the G.Mate Yopy and the Motorola A760. I count 29 different varieties of commercial mobile Linux that have existed over the years, and there are probably many more that I missed. There have been many different waves of mobile Linux, which at the time looked like they might become the next big thing, including EZX, MotoMagx, Maemo, LiMo, Moblin, Meego, Tizen, Firefox OS, webOS, Ubuntu Touch and Sailfish OS. For years Motorola experimented with different Linux varieties that were based on the idea of using Java apps available in a community store, so Google’s Android was hardly unique, but it was the flavor of mobile Linux which succeeded. Today, all of them are often lumped together under the label of “Linux” as a separate category from Android, but Tizen and Firefox OS are just as distinct architecturally as Android from a standard desktop Linux distro.

The mobile Linux operating systems live on, although they are less visible today. Much of the MeeGo code that Nokia created for the N9, continues to be developed by the tiny Finnish company, the Jolla Group, which is once again selling phones with its Sailfish OS. Firefox OS, which was abandoned by Mozilla Foundation in 2016, was reborn in 2017 as proprietary KaiOS for low-end phones without touch screens, but that market is slowly disappearing as Android now reaches even the cheapest segments of the mobile phone market. Ubuntu Touch, which was abandoned by Canonical in 2017, lives on as a community-based project under the volunteers at UBports. Even, webOS and Tizen still exist, although they are no longer used as mobile operating systems. webOS runs LG TVs and Tizen is used in Samsung TVs.

Although it doesn’t generate many headlines in the tech press, a tiny Linux phone market still exists. Purism, PINE64, FuriLabs, Jolla, Jolla-Devices, Volla and PrivacyPortal (plus Brax in the future) all sell phones with some flavor of Linux preinstalled. The number of people buying Linux phones today is fewer than in 2020-22 when PINE64 was launching the PinePhone and PinePhone Pro, but there are actually more companies selling Linux phones than there was 5 years ago. There are good reasons to believe that many of the problems that plagued Linux phones in the past are going to be overcome in the future.

The SoC dilemma: weak but long lived vs powerful but short lived

In the past, the available hardware choices limited the viability of Linux phones. Systems-on-a-Chip (SoC’s) which support Linux are generally used in single-board-computers (SBC’s), TV setup boxes, internet of things (IoT) devices and embedded microprocessors in industrial and automotive applications, where the price points are lower, so their performance is generally weaker and they are less energy efficient than the typical mobile SoC designed for smartphones, because they are fabbed on older process nodes. However, they offer long-term support, because they are used in applications that have long product life cycles. For example, automobiles contain dozens of SoC’s and they typically takes 3 to 5 years just to design and need to be able to run for the next 20 years. In contrast, the mobile SoC’s with Android support are very powerful, but they are only produced for 1 to 3 years.

If the designers of Linux phones want to be able to run a Linux kernel (as opposed to an Android kernel), most of their options offer little processing power, poor energy efficiency and poor thermals. If they want to avoid proprietary blobs as much as possible, they either have to choose an older SoC which the community has been worked on for years to iron out the bugs in the free/open source drivers (e.g., the Allwinner A64 in the PinePhone), or they have to spend years patching the Linux kernel to properly support a newer SoC (as Purism did with the NXP i.MX 8M Quad in the Librem 5). If they decide that it is too much trouble to send their patches to mainline Linux, then it will be harder to support their hardware in the future, because they will have to keep applying those same patches to each new Linux kernel release. Purism chose to upstream their changes to mainline Linux, whereas the volunteers working on the PinePhone’s kernel generally didn’t.

The chipmakers like NXP, Rockchip, Allwinner, Amlogic and Broadcom who make SoC’s with Linux support simply don’t generate enough revenue to justify using a leading-edge process node in their chips. Even thought they can sell a Linux SoC for 10 to 15 years, they still won’t sell enough to recoup the extra $400 – $600 million that it would cost to use a 3nm process, and the costs keep going up with each new generation of process node. It is enormously expensive to design a chip at the cutting edge of the silicon industry. Silicon Analysts estimates that fabbing a wafer at TSMC costs an average of $19,500 at a 3nm node, but only $3000 at a 28nm node. Most Linux SoC’s are low-priced chips with very thin margins, so they have to sell millions of them to make much profit. Some Linux SoC makers like NXP focus on specialty markets, so they they have higher margins, but they tend not to sell many of them, so the profits are still limited.

Another way that chipmakers reduce their costs is by using older generations of Cortex cores, which have lower licensing fees from ARM, and by using lots of low-power Cortex-A5 series cores, rather than the higher-power Cortex-A7 and Cortex-X series cores, which have higher licensing fees. NXP was clearly employing these cost cutting strategies with its i.MX 9 series processors. The most powerful chip in the series is the i.MX 95, which contains six Cortex-A55 cores, when it would have made more sense to use two Cortex-A78 cores for better performance and four Cortex-A55 cores for low power. The i.MX 95 was fabbed on a 16nm FinFET node, which is a slight regression compared to Samsung’s 14nm node used in the previous i.MX 8M Plus processor. Another example of this cost cutting was the decision by Broadcom to use older Cortex cores and larger process nodes in its BCM2836 (40nm, 4x Cortex-A7), BCM2837 (40nm, 4x Cortex-A53), BCM2711 (28nm, 4x Cortex-A72) and BCM2712 (16nm, 4x Cortex-A76), despite knowing that millions of these chips would be sold (e.g. in the Raspberry Pi 2, 3, 4 and 5, respectively). Even Nvidia, which is the world’s richest chipmaker due to the AI boom, appears to be avoiding the costs of using a leading-edge process node in its Tegra SoC. It canceled its planned Tegra Atlan series which was announced in April 2021, and still hasn’t released its Tegra Thor series, which was announced in September 2022. Its Tegra Orin series which was announced in March 2018 is now getting long in the tooth using an 8nm node.

In contrast, the smartphone market, which sold 1.25 billion units in 2025, has enormous volumes, and phone makers are willing to pay much higher prices for processors, especially for higher-end models, which allows Qualcomm, MediaTek, Apple, Samsung, Google, Xiaomi and Huawei to make the enormous investment in designing mobile SoC’s for an expensive 3nm process node. Integrated mobile SoC’s such as the Qualcomm Snapdragon and MediaTek Dimensity have so much volume, that they can make a profit despite the fact that they generally are only produced for 2 to 3 years. The flagship models (e.g. the Snapdragon 8 series and Dimensity 9000 series) lose most of their market after the first year, so SoC makers have to charge much higher prices to cover the enormous costs of using a leading-edge process node.

In addition, the integrated mobile SoC’s that run Android incorporate many additional functions, such as WiFi, Bluetooth, cellular modem, GPS/GNSS, audio DAC, charge controller and USB-C controller, which require separate chips on Linux phones like the PinePhone and Librem 5. This makes the circuit boards for these phones much more expensive to design, because they can’t just take a standard reference design from Qualcomm or MediaTek and tweak it. They have to custom design their circuit boards, which requires two to three times more components than the circuit board for a typical smartphone. The Librem 5 contains 74 integrated circuits (IC’s) and its 4 circuit boards have a total of 1267 components, making it the most complex phone ever created. The six chips (i.MX 8M Quad, RS9116, BM818, Teseo-LIV3F, WM8962 and bq25895) that the Librem 5 uses in place of an integrated mobile SoC occupy a total of 1483.2 mm2, which is 10 times the area of a Snapdragon 8. Purism had to use components as small as 0201 and use 10 layers to cram everything into the Librem 5’s main circuit board, which had to go through roughly a dozen iterations to get right. Even a minimal Linux phone like the PinePhone, which was designed to be as economical as possible, has 24 ICs and a total of 627 components on its circuit board, making it more complex than most Android smartphones, which typically have 300 to 400 components.

Adding all these extra components makes Linux phones more expensive to design and produce, but it also makes them suck more power, since it takes more energy to run half a dozen chips at larger node sizes than one integrated mobile SoC fabbed on a ≤4nm node, which has been optimized for energy efficiency. It is hard to coordinate all the extra chips in Linux phones to get them to enter lower power modes and sleep modes to conserve their batteries. Add in an SoC with an older node size between 28 and 8 nm that hasn’t been optimized for battery usage, and there is no way that Linux phones can match the battery life of Android phones.

The RK3588S changes the game for Linux phones

Many of the Linux SoC makers have decided that they shouldn’t even bother building chips with the CPU and GPU performance needed for a modern computing device. NXP, Amlogic and Broadcom simply aren’t interested in building competitive SoC’s. However, Rockchip fundamentally changed the prospects for making a decent Linux phone when it released the RK3588 and its lower-power RK3588S variant in 2022. With four 2.4Ghz Cortex-A76 cores and four 1.8GHz Cortex-A55 cores and a Mali-G610 MC4 graphics, there finally was a Linux SoC on the market with enough processing power in an SoC to make an acceptable Linux smartphone.

The Liberux NEXX and the Dawndrums Divine D. are two Linux phones currently being designed with the RK3588S. Purism just announced on its forum that its next gen phone “is actively being designed,” which won’t be based on the i.MX platform like the Librem 5 and Liberty, so it is likely to be based on the RK3588S as well.

Of course, the RK3588S’s performance isn’t going to impress anyone used to an Android phone. The RK3588 and RK3588S are fabbed on a 8nm process node, which is four generations behind today’s state of the art at 2nm. Today’s low-end Snapdragon 4 Gen 4 fabbed at 4nm has 25% better single core CPU performance than the RK3588. (See the table of SoC’s below.) The RK3588S has similar performance to the RK3588 over short bursts, but its performance is 10%-15% less over periods longer than 30 seconds. By the time the Linux phones based on the RK3588S hit the market in a couple years time, they will have significantly worse performance than every Android smartphone on the market, but this difference probably won’t be a limiting factor for most people who aren’t 3D gaming or shooting high-resolution video. At a certain point, more processing power has diminishing utility, and the RK3588S crosses that threshold for most people.

Where the older process tech will be significant is in terms of their energy consumption. A phone sporting the RK3588S will run hotter and have worse battery life than phones using integrated mobile SoC’s from Qualcomm, MediaTek, UNISOC, etc. The challenge is to dissipate the extra heat. The PinePhone’s SoC and cellular modem get very hot because they do not have a good heat spreader. The Librem 5’s SoC is joined with thermal paste to the back plate of the LCD, which avoids overheating the SoC, but causes the touchscreen and aluminum frame to become hot to the touch. A Linux phone with the RK3358S will need some kind of heat dissipation, but it is unlikely that a Linux phone maker can afford to include a vapor chamber, since those have to be specially designed and would be very expensive for a phone of limited production. The RK3588S will need throttling to fit within the power and thermal envelope of a phone.

At first, the mainline Linux support for the RK3588 was very limited. Rockchip never published the documentation for the chip on its opensource.rock-chips.com site, and Rockchip took down that site at the end of 2025. On December 21, 2024, Jeff Geerling, the most influential reviewer in the Raspberry Pi alternative space, reported on X:

I was told Rockchip no longer considers RK3588 to be an ‘open source’ chip. In practice, that means Rockchip no longer contributes RK3588 code to open-source projects and they also decided not to sell RK3588 directly to SBC vendors.

On the other hand, Rockchip is still updating its public kernel code for the RK3588 at Github. Collabora has been toiling away for years to add mainline Linux support for the RK3588, and Collabora lists Rockchip as one of its partners, so Rockchip hasn’t totally abandoned the Linux community. Collabora recently added mainline Linux support for the video capture unit and MIPI CSI2 interface in the RK3588. Now Collabora is working with Ideas on Board and Rockchip to create an new image signal processor (ISP) driver for all the RK35xx chips. Collabora has gotten the hardware video decoder working for VP8, VP9, H.264 and H.265, and is now working on the hardware video encoder for H.264.

Four years after the RK3588S was released, there is now enough support for the chip in mainline Linux, that an RK3588S phone can be created running free/open source drivers. The RK3588S needs to execute a proprietary Synopsys DDR timing training blob at boot. The RK3588S can now use the free Panthor driver for the GPU, but it requires the proprietary mali_csffw.bin firmware, which is loaded from the /lib/firmware/ directory at boot. All the other blobs for the RK3588S have either been replaced or they aren’t necessary. There is now a FOSS driver for the NPU. The proprietary MPP library for hardware video encoding can be replaced with software video encoding, and Collabora is working on free drivers for the ISP and hardware video encode, so software video processing and encoding probably won’t be necessary in the future. Collabora has developed a FOSS version for the Trusted Firmware-A (TF-A), that can replace the proprietary bl31.elf firmware. The HDMI blob in the bl31.elf isn’t necessary if using DisplayPort Alt Mode for video out. The proprietary bl32.bin firmware is not necessary if not using the hardware-enforced security features or encryption keys.
If Purism uses the RK3588S in its next phone, it is unlikely that Purism will attempt to obtain the FSF’s RYF certification by storing blobs on a separate NOR Flash chip and executing them with a secondary processor, like it did with the Librem 5, because the RK3588S doesn’t have a secondary low-power processor like the Cortex-M4 in the i.MX 8M Quad.

There are good prospects that Collabora will eventually get all the RK3588S’s hardware supported with mainline Linux drivers, and until then, the RK3588S has enough processing power in the GPU and CPU to process and encode images and video in software, so a phone built on the RK3588S can take photos and shoot video like a normal smartphone, although it will be slower and use more energy. In contrast, previous phones using a Linux kernel simply didn’t have enough processing power to offer decent cameras. Taking photos on the PinePhone is painfully slow, and the Millipixels app on the Librem 5 pauses for 3 to 4 seconds after taking each photo. Because the Librem 5’s i.MX 8M Quad processor lacks an ISP, audio DSP and hardware video encoder, it takes roughly 10 times as long to process and encode a 720p video on the Librem 5 as the length of the video, and it’s about 50 times longer on the PinePhone, due to its antiquated Allwinner A64 processor and significantly slower RAM and eMMC.

Aside from the RK3588S, there aren’t many other options on the market to make a good Linux phone. The closest option is Nvidia’s Tegra Orin NX or Orin Nano Super, which only contain Cortex-A78 cores. They lack low-power Cortex-A55 cores and they aren’t very energy efficient. They sport newer tech than the Cortex-A76 cores in the RK3588S, but the Tegra Orin was fabbed on a 8nm node just like the RK3588S and the Tegra Orin’s lower clock rate limits its single-core performance. The Tegra Orin is also much worse in terms of software freedom, requiring proprietary blobs in the initial bootloader, the secondary bootloader, Boot Configuration Table, USB firmware, HDMI/DisplayPort configuration, ARM Trusted Firmware and the GPU userspace driver. Many Linux users can ignore the blobs in the Linux device tree, but it harder to ignore Nvidia’s GPU blob in the userspace.

Another option is the Allwinner A733 at 12nm, which offers less performance with dual 2.0Ghz Cortex-A76 cores and six 1.79GHz Cortex-A55 low-power cores. Allwinner stopped collaborating with the Linux community years ago, and has frequently violated the GPL 2.0 license by not publishing its Linux source code, so the A733 probably won’t be a viable option, although Allwinner has made some comments about intending to collaborate with the community in the future. Another option is the NXP i.MX 95, which does have mainline Linux support, but its performance on a 16nm node with six low-power Cortex-A55 cores is poor and not a good value for the money.

The PinePhone 2 was expected to use the more economical Rockchip RK3566, which is fabbed on an older 22nm node. However, so many volunteer developers abandoned PINE64 in 2022, that it is unlikely that the Hong Kong-based company will be launching any new models in the foreseeable future. The production of PINE64’s Linux devices are currently on hold due to the high RAM and eMMC prices caused by the AI boom, but part of the reason is that PINE64 can’t raise prices on many of its devices, which are only half-functional, because many of the community groups, who worked on the PinePhone, are no longer developing the software to support PINE64’s newer devices.

Another reason the RK3588 is the preferred option is because Rockchip is promising to provide a successor chip, the RK3668 with four Cortex-A730 cores and six Cortex-A530 cores at a 5 or 6 nm node in 2027, so it should be possible to keep upgrading the phone in the future. Purism invested heavily in supporting the 28nm i.MX 8M Quad in the Librem 5, thinking that it would be possible to upgrade to a future 14nm version of the SoC, but NXP decided to eliminate half the cores in the GPU and remove DisplayPort support in the 14nm i.MX 8M Plus, so Purism couldn’t upgrade its phone in the same processor family. Given that the cost of fabbing on smaller process nodes keeps rising, it is unlikely that any of the other chipmakers will launch a new chip to challenge the RK3588’s performance in the near future.

The new option of Linux phones using a Qualcomm IoT SoC

In the past, the only way to create a phone running on a Linux kernel was to design a complex device containing many separate chips. Historically Qualcomm didn’t bother making powerful processors for its SoC’s that supported Linux. However, there has been increasing demand for more powerful Internet of Things processors that can handle AI and lots of image processing from multiple video feeds. Unlike short-lived smartphones and tablets, IoT devices have long product lives, so they are better suited to use Linux, rather than Android which is much harder to support over time. In March 2023, Qualcomm dramatically improved the prospects for Linux phones with the announcement that its upcoming 6nm QCM6490 processor with an integrated cellular modem would support four operating systems (Android, Linux, Ubuntu and Windows IoT Enterprise).

Then, the San Diego-based company announced its new Product Longevity Program, which would both sell and provide software support for the QCM6490 until July 2036. Both the FairPhone 5 and SHIFTphone 8 were designed around the QCM6490, due to the environmental benefits to its long support, and that long support is exactly what Linux phones also need, because it takes so long to bring a Linux phone to market and it needs to sell for many years to recoup the high investment in a product that has limited annual sales. The Fairphone 5 with the QCM6490 (1x 2.7Ghz Cortex-A78, 3x 2.4GHz Cortex-A78, 4x 1.9Ghz Cortex-A55) was criticized for its poor benchmarks and poor battery life compared to other Android phones. However, the QCM6490 offers significantly better CPU and GPU performance and better energy efficiency than the RK3588S.

The subsequent QCM4490 and QCM8850, which are fabbed on a newer 4nm node, offer lower and higher power options than the QCM6490. The QCM4490 (2x 2.4GHz Cortex-A78, 6x 2.0GHz Cortex-A55) has almost as good single-core performance as the QCM6490 and is more energy efficient, but its support ends in April 2030, which is too short for a Linux phone. The QCM8850 probably could be downclocked to fit within the power envelope of a Linux phone, but its support ends in April 2033, so the longer-lived QCM6490 is probably the better option for a Linux phone.

The benefit of using one of these IoT processors, which Qualcomm has rebranded as “Dragonwing“, is that they make it significantly easier to design a phone and bring it to market, since they incorporate so much functionality in one chip, which reduces the complexity of the phone’s circuit board. Qualcomm provides reference designs that can be customized, so designing a Linux phone with a Dragonwing processor should be much easier and require fewer circuit board iterations and less testing.

A company with limited resources could contract with SHIFT or Fairphone to produce their phones and then install Linux, similar to the way that both Murena and iodé sell Fairphones and SHIFTphones and install their AOSP variants focused on privacy on the phones. Not only would this avoid the time and cost of designing the hardware, but it would allow the Linux phone to be marketed for its environmental and ethical benefits. Fairphone or SHIFT could also be contracted to provide the warranty service for the phone.

Qualcomm provides free/open source drivers for its Snapdragon and Dragonwing processors, and over time many of these processors will be partially supported in mainline Linux. However, the Qualcomm drivers depend on many proprietary blobs. The Adreno A660 GPU uses a blob to accelerate the 3D graphics. The audio digital signal processor (aDSP) uses a blob to handle audio decoding and processing. A compute blob is used by the DSP and NPU for tasks like machine learning.
